title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether adding a deterministic network verifier to a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Using N = 240 paired intents (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across paired arms), the run completed as planned (planned episodes = 480, completed = 480, model calls used = 240). All 240 paired tasks were scored safe under both arms: baseline = 240/240 = 1.0, guarded = 240/240 = 1.0; paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. No validator‑triggered repairs were applied because every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator. We report the preregistered design, exact execution accounting, and a failure‑analytic interpretation of the null paired outcome, and we provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future emulation‑grounded NetOps evaluations.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into concrete device configuration and to automate NetOps workflows. Execution‑grounded evaluations that place LLM agents into emulated networks reveal planning and workflow failures that token‑level metrics miss [1]. A recurring operational mitigation is a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pattern: produce a candidate configuration, apply a deterministic validator, and invoke repair when the validator signals a violation [2,3]. We preregistered and ran a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment measuring whether adding a deterministic verifier (with up to one validator‑triggered repair) reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from a single LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline when the same initial LLM candidate is shared across paired arms. Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered paired confirmatory run (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) executed on an emulation benchmark; (2) archival of per‑call traces, execution accounting, and analysis artifacts; and (3) a failure‑analytic interpretation of a null paired outcome together with concrete experiment‑design recommendations.
sections.related_work: Emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks and closed‑loop agent evaluations demonstrate that multi‑step planning and execution faults arise in task‑oriented NetOps agents and motivate executable testing frameworks [1]. The generate‑and‑validate (or generate–validate–repair) architecture recurs across configuration repair and program‑repair literature and is reported to reduce syntactic and some semantic failures when validator coverage and repair search are sufficient [2,4]. Recent surveys and position pieces advocate tool augmentation, verifier gating, and uncertainty calibration for agentic systems, while noting the need for tighter empirical evaluation of verifier impact under distribution shift and adversarial prompts [3,5]. These prior results establish the motivation and the evaluation desiderata we operationalized in a paired, emulation‑grounded design.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe‑apply rate). Design and sampling: N = 240 distinct tasks executed as paired episodes (baseline LLM‑only vs guarded GVR). Task composition: in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial 20% (48). Generation semantics and adapter contract: per the registered adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) we used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused for both arms; only a validator‑triggered repair (at most one permitted per task in the guarded arm) could create a paired divergence. (Explicit consequence: under shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired contrast only tests validator/repair effects conditional on initial candidates failing validation; if every shared initial candidate passes validation the guarded and baseline final outputs will be identical.) Models and runtime: the declared_model_version was "gpt-5-mini" and the archived execution model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset); archived provider call metadata were recorded for every model call. Guarding, validator, and repair budget: the guarded arm used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Budget, retries, and stopping: planned_episode_count = 480, maximum_model_calls = 480, preregistered retry policy for infra failures allowed up to two recovery attempts per failed task; missingness and exclusion rules (including handling of verifier PASS vs simulator unsafe mismatches) were specified in the preregistration. Scoring and analysis: each episode was deterministically executed in the emulator and scored safe (0) or unsafe (1). Primary analysis used the registered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor with 10,000 bootstrap resamples (seed = 1729) to estimate paired percentile CIs and an exact McNemar two‑sided test for the paired contingency table. All raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts were archived.
sections.results: Execution accounting and reconciliation: the registered adapter completed the planned run: planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240; hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 (one shared initial generation per task) and model_calls_used = 240 (provider call audit reports stage_counts {shared_initial_generation: 240}). Primary binary outcomes: baseline_success_count = 240/240 (success rate 1.0), guarded_success_count = 240/240 (success rate 1.0). Paired contingency: n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Inference: paired difference = 0.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Repair and call activity: no validator‑triggered repairs were applied in any guarded episode (repair_attempts = 0); consequently guarded and baseline final configurations were identical for every pair because the single shared initial candidate passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in each task. Missingness and flags: analysis/missingness_summary.csv and analysis/contamination_summary.csv show zero infra failures and zero flagged 'possible false‑safe' items; therefore no preregistered exclusions affected the primary analysis.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the preregistered primary hypothesis (H1: GVR reduces unsafe‑apply rate relative to LLM‑only) is not supported by these data. Critically, under shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm can only differ when the shared initial candidate fails validation or when a repair is applied; because every shared initial candidate passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to alter any paired outcome and the paired contrast is degenerate (no discordant pairs). Statistical consequence: n10 = n01 = 0 yields a degenerate McNemar test and a zero‑width bootstrap CI, which are faithful to the observed execution trace rather than indicating an analysis error. Design recommendations (artifact‑grounded): (1) To measure verifier benefit in a paired framework, relax shared_initial_candidate semantics (allow independent initial generation per arm) or permit an expanded repair budget and repair/search strategy so generator variability can produce validator failures in at least one arm. (2) Strengthen adversary adaptivity and attacker sampling (beyond a single preregistered attacker seed) when testing guard efficacy against prompt injection. (3) Broaden deterministic verifier semantic coverage and instrument routine cross‑checks (verifier PASS vs simulator outcome) to measure false‑safe rates. (4) Report repair counts, model‑call budgets, and latency to evaluate operational cost trade‑offs. Threats to validity: internal validity is constrained by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single‑model execution; construct validity is limited by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule coverage; external validity is limited by the emulation corpus and single‑model scope; conclusion validity is constrained because the observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 rendered the preregistered paired contrast untestable in this run. All artifacts are archived for reanalysis under alternative generation semantics.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Every paired episode was safe under both LLM‑only and guarded arms, producing a paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Deterministic reconciliation confirms that no validator‑triggered repairs occurred because the single shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator for all tasks. The null paired result is informative: under shared_initial_candidate semantics a deterministic verifier can only affect paired outcomes when initial candidates fail validation or when the design permits generator variability between arms. We provide the preregistration, execution manifest, per‑call traces, and analysis artifacts to support follow‑up experiments that vary generation semantics, adversary strength, and verifier coverage.

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: The experiment used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Runtime sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset); unset temperature does not imply deterministic sampling by the hosted provider and sampling nondeterminism remains possible; all model‑call metadata were archived. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock; a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the lock; no manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred post‑lock. Preregistered generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms), so only validator‑triggered repairs could create paired divergences; this semantics is explicitly used and reported in Methods and Results. Execution accounting (archived): planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240. Immutable master prompt: the initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Reproducibility pointer: archived execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are available in the execution bundle (see execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/).
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompt templates, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidates failing validation.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed attacker protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
